title: Teenagers from Outer Space

evidence.note: Secondary sources say the film lapsed into the public domain in 1987 after no renewal in its 28th year. I could not reach a primary record. I found no CCE renewal listing, and renewals due 1978 or later are not in the printed CCE. I did not run a publicrecords.copyright.gov search. The 1959 registration volume is on archive.org (Motion Pictures and Filmstrips Jan-Dec 1959), but I did not read its entry. Notice on the print was not checked.
evidence.source: Wikipedia article on the film (secondary); Internet Archive CCE 1959 Motion Pictures volume

evidence.note: Sources disagree on the music credit, and I could not settle who wrote the score or whether it is original or library music. I name no composer here. The score's own rights are unconfirmed and may differ from the film's, so confirm them before reuse.
Writer-director-producer Tom Graeff wrote the film himself. I found no source work that would carry its own term. The story's status follows the film's copyright, which is unconfirmed.

editorial:
Teenagers from Outer Space is a 1959 black-and-white science-fiction film. Tom Graeff produced, wrote and directed it through Tom Graeff Productions, and Warner Bros. distributed it. In the story, a young alien falls for an Earth girl and tries to stop his cohorts' invasion. The Internet Archive lists a full 85-minute copy. Reusers want it for its cult standing and its Mystery Science Theater 3000 afterlife.

The rights question rests on renewal. Secondary sources say the copyright was not renewed in 1987, so the film lapsed. This dossier could not confirm that from the Copyright Office record or a renewal-year catalog, so the print is marked undetermined. Check the Stanford renewal database and the Copyright Office public catalog yourself before relying on it. Even if the print is free, the score's own rights are unconfirmed, and any edit with added material, such as the MST3K version, is a separate question.
faq: Is Teenagers from Outer Space safe to reuse in the US?

Not confirmed here. Secondary sources say the copyright lapsed for lack of renewal in 1987. I could not confirm that against the Copyright Office record, and I did not check the print for a copyright notice. Run the Stanford and Copyright Office searches linked above before publishing.
Can I use the Mystery Science Theater 3000 version?

Not on the strength of the film's status alone. Riffing and added commentary are separate material. Use a plain black-and-white copy, such as the Internet Archive item, and confirm the score's rights separately.
